major.name: Media Industries and Communication - BA

items.text: Any other course numbered in the COMM 106 series (offerings may change each year).

items.label: Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
FOUR additional upper-division electives (COMM 101–190)
items.notes: Only ONE course of COMM 198 or 199 may be applied to satisfy an upper-division elective for the major. AIP 197 must be petitioned for approval for the major and may only be applied to satisfy an upper-division elective.

items.label: Practice course in residence within the communication department
items.notes: At least ONE practice course must be taken in residence at UC San Diego, within the communication department.

items.text: Petitions for transfer or study abroad credits will be considered, particularly if they match a course on the list.

items.label: Second practice course
items.notes: The other practice course may be taken at the lower-division level; ONE practice course may be taken outside of the communication department.

narrative: All courses taken to satisfy major requirements must be taken for a letter grade. A grade of C– or better is required for all courses for the major.
Courses marked * must be taken at UC San Diego: COMM 10, COMM 106, COMM 100A-B-C, the COMM 106 series courses, the three COMM 160–190 electives, and the communication-department practice courses.
Outside practice courses marked † (VIS 142, VIS 148, MGT 103, MGT 162, MGT 172, SOCI 104Q, SOCI 109M) require upper-division standing.

nodes.title: Introduction to Python for Biologists
nodes.description: Introductory class for biology students interested in using Python for data analysis and visualization. Course covers the basics of programming in Python and introduces students to various implementations of Python analyses for biological data such as time series and images. Students will use their own laptops.

nodes.title: Culture, Art, and Technology 1
nodes.prereq_text: Sixth College students only; completion of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement.

items.text: Sixth College students only
completion of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement

nodes.description: Lower-division composition course teaching critical reading and drafting by examining how culture, art, and technology have intersected in the past.

nodes.title: Culture, Art, and Technology 2

items.text: Sixth College students only

nodes.description: Lower-division writing-intensive course foregrounding argumentation, revision, and writing as process by examining case studies of culture, art, and technology interacting in the present moment.

nodes.title: Culture, Art, and Technology 3

items.text: Sixth College students only

nodes.description: Lower-division writing- and research-intensive course focusing on collaboration, research, and art-making by speculating on how the relationships between culture, art, and technology will be transformed in the future.

nodes.title: Critical Approaches in Community Practice
nodes.prereq_text: Eighth College students only; completion of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement.

items.text: Eighth College students only
completion of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement

nodes.description: Introduces ethical partnership across complex social, historical, and political positions. The course addresses contested framings of community and participation through practical examples, theoretical conceptions, and empirical studies. Students will give close attention to shared circumstance and negotiation of power relations. Must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Eighth College general-education requirements.

nodes.title: Cultivating Community-Informed Practices

items.text: Eighth College students only

nodes.description: This course introduces students to writing as a community-informed endeavor. Students will develop writing practices to engage in respectful, meaningful, ethical, and reciprocal community partnerships. Using participatory action and community-rooted research, students will develop reading, writing, and thinking practices that recognize, honor, and foster community knowledge. Must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Eighth College general-education requirements.

nodes.title: Introduction to Cognitive Science
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: A team-taught course highlighting development of the field and the broad range of topics covered in the major. Example topics include addiction, analogy, animal cognition, human-computer interaction, language, neuroimaging, neural networks, reasoning, robots, and real-world applications.

nodes.title: Introduction to Computing
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Covers the fundamental concepts that underlie all programming languages and provides an introduction to the essential information about algorithms and data structures. Students design and implement web applications using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Photoshop. No previous programming experience is required.

nodes.title: Hands-on Computing
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introductory-level course that will give students hands-on experience with robotics, Python programming, and integrating cognitive principles for robot interaction.

nodes.title: Introduction to Data Science
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Concepts of data and its role in science will be introduced, as well as the ideas behind data-mining, text-mining, machine learning, and graph theory, and how scientists and companies are leveraging those methods to uncover new insights into human cognition.

nodes.title: Introduction to Research Methods
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduction to the scientific method. Methods of knowledge acquisition, research questions, hypotheses, operational definitions, variables, control. Observation, levels of measurement, reliability, validity. Experimentation and design: between-groups, within-subjects, quasi-experimental, factorial, single-subject. Correlational and observational studies. Ethics in research.

nodes.title: Introduction to Python
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course

nodes.title: Introduction to Communication
groups: Lower-Division Courses (two courses)
nodes.description: This course is an introduction to the history, theory, and practice of communication. Topics covered include language literacy, representation, semiotics, mediated technologies, institutional formations, and social interaction. Course work may involve media production (for example, writing, video and media production, or performance). No credit for COMM 10 if taken after COMM 10R.

nodes.title: Analysis of Audio/Visual Media: Form, Style, and Meaning
groups: Lower-Division Courses (two courses): ONE course from the following
nodes.description: This course builds the critical skills to understand, analyze, interpret audio/visual media by introducing students to the basic vocabulary and grammar of audio and moving image texts—how they create meaning through compositional form and narrative style—and key critical methodologies for interpreting media culture. Concepts covered will lay the groundwork for continued study in scholarly communication areas and hands-on sound, film/video, and/or social media production. No credit for COMM 20 if taken after COMM 20R.

nodes.title: Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
groups: Lower-Division Courses (two courses): ONE course from the following
nodes.description: The role of digital communication in a democratic system, and the ways mass media both facilitate and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere. By exploring today’s digital communication dynamics, students will have the opportunity to become more mindful, active consumers of media and to feel empowered to be engaged participants in public life. No credit for COMM 30 if taken after COMM 30GS or COMM 30R.

nodes.title: Global Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
nodes.description: This course focuses on the role of journalism in a global system, and the ways mass media both contribute to and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere and effective political process. With a focus on American as well as international news media, we will examine theories and functions of journalism as well as current issues facing today’s news producers. This is a Global Seminar course. No credit for COMM 30GS if taken after COMM 30 or COMM 30R. Program or materials fees may apply.

nodes.title: Introduction to Promotional Communication
groups: Lower-Division Courses (two courses): ONE course from the following
nodes.description: A critical-cultural communication introduction to fields of practice that publicize, promote, or increase awareness of brands, ideas, products, and causes. Exploration of public communication industries and practices, the pressures that shape these industries and practices, and their implications for culture and society. Course will address major promotional industries such as advertising, public relations, marketing, and social media.

nodes.title: Communication, the Person, and Everyday Life
groups: Required Upper-Division Courses (three courses): TWO courses from the following
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to processes of interaction within lived and built environments. It includes historical survey of theories and methods including actor network-theory, conversation analysis, ethnography, ethnomethodology, cultural linguistics, performance, and social cognition. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (for example, in-context observation and research or audio/video production). No credit for COMM 100A if taken after COMM 100AR.

nodes.title: Communication, Culture, and Representation
groups: Required Upper-Division Courses (three courses): TWO courses from the following
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to the history of representation, surveying a range of theories and methods that have been used to understand and shape representational practices. The course will focus on relationships between form and content across various representational genres in shifting cultural contexts. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (e.g., image-making or video/media production). No credit for COMM 100BR if taken after COMM 100B.

nodes.title: Communication, Institutions, and Power
groups: Required Upper-Division Courses (three courses): TWO courses from the following
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to structures of communication formed at the intersection of the state, the economy, and civil society. It includes a historical survey of communication and media industries; legal and policy-based arenas; and civic, political, and social organizations. Students will learn to assess the movement of power through these institutions and its effect in shaping society, culture, and politics. No credit for COMM 100C if taken after COMM 100CR.

nodes.title: Introduction to Audiovisual Media Practices
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This upper-division course is required as the gateway to all future communication media production courses. Students will learn about contemporary media practices such as film, video, digital/online, and social media production, and how these practices are formed by technical and social constraints. In the studio portion of this course, students will work hands-on with video and new media equipment to apply what they have learned.

nodes.title: Production of Activist Media
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10 or COMM 20 or COMM 30 or COMM 30GS or COMM 40 and COMM 101.
nodes.description: In this course, we ask what techniques, strategies, and platforms we might engage to present messages in an impactful and ethical way. We engage with different media forms each quarter, maintaining an emphasis on production and documentary storytelling. The aim of this class is to demystify the idea of a “media activist” by guiding students through the development of their own media activism.

nodes.title: MPL: Nonlinear/Digital Editing
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This hands-on post-production course introduces students to the art and practice of editing. Approaches to montage will be analyzed, discussed, and critically applied. This course is project-intensive, and will prepare students to edit using digital non-linear editing systems. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MPL: Documentary Sketchbook
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Digital video is the medium used in this class both as a production technology and as a device to explore the theory and practice of documentary production. Technical demonstrations, lectures, production exercises, and readings will emphasize the interrelation between production values and ethics, problems of representation, and documentary history. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MPL: Sound Production and Manipulation
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This hands-on course serves as an introduction to sound production, design, and editing. Students create projects by recording original sounds and editing on a digital audio workstation. We consider the potential of sound in film, radio, TV, and on the web by reviewing work and reading sound theory. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Audio Story and Podcasting Practicum
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Production-oriented course involving diverse audio media forms. Critically analyze journalistic podcasts, features, documentaries, diaries, place-casts, and news shorts to evaluate what makes for compelling and effective audio as a contemporary storytelling form. Students will gain technical and production skills to facilitate their own creativity in the audio sphere. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Practicum in New Media and Community Life
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: A combined lecture/lab in a specially designed after-school setting in southeastern San Diego working with children and adults. Students design new media and produce special projects, and explore issues related to human development, social justice, and community life. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Studio Television
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course offers students the opportunity to produce and engage in critical discussions around various television production formats. We will study and produce a variety of projects, including public service announcements, panel programs, scripted drama, and performance productions. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: Introduction to Media Industries
groups: Required Upper-Division Courses (three courses)
nodes.description: Introduction to topics that arise across various media industries, including media economics, ownership and consolidation in media, media regulation and deregulation, media technologies, creative labor, intellectual property, financialization, globalization, and ethics in media. Engage directly with current events, read recent coverage in the trade press, and learn to analyze contemporary media companies and systems. No credit for COMM 106 if taken after COMM 106R.

nodes.title: Streaming Media Industries
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: This course examines the ecosystem of streaming media from the perspective of power and political economy, focusing on the key corporations that shape our experience of it. How do corporations control the infrastructure of streaming media? How have streams, platforms, and algorithms changed our society? What is the effect of streaming media on creatives, laborers, and producers of content? What opportunities and obstacles are there in streaming media for more diversity and equality? No credit for COMM 106B if taken after COMM 106BR.

nodes.title: Data and AI Industries
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: Advances in AI and data science raise new and old issues about the role data plays in society. Students will learn how institutions (especially cultural industries) collect data, make predictions, and automate labor. Students will critically engage with data/AI practices and cultural representations of data/AI, discussing issues like privacy, power, bias, representation, regulation, and labor. Students will learn high-level tech concepts, but this class has no programming requirement.

nodes.title: The Film Industry
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: A study of the social organization of the film industry throughout its history. Who makes films, by what criteria, and for what audience? The changing relationships between studios, producers, directors, writers, actors, editors, censors, distributors, audience, and subject matter of the films will be explored. No credit for COMM 106F if taken after COMM 106FR.

nodes.title: Tourism: Global Industry and Cultural Form
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: The largest industry in the world has far-reaching cultural ramifications. We will explore tourism’s history and its contemporary cultural effects, taking the perspective of the “toured” as well as that of the tourist. No credit for COMM 106G if taken after COMM 106GR.

nodes.title: Internet Industry
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: The political economy of the emergent internet industry, charted through analysis of its hardware, software, and services components. The course specifies leading trends and changing institutional outcomes by relating the internet industry to the adjoining media, telecommunications, and computer industries. No credit for COMM 106I if taken after COMM 106IR.

nodes.title: Advertising and Society
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: Advertising as a commercial and social force. The development of advertising, branding, and consumer culture in the United States; the history and political economy of advertising in mass and digital media; semiotics and representation in advertisements; influencers, authenticity, and the monetization of self and community; subversion and rebellion within systems of advertisement and promotion. Renumbered from COMM 109D. No credit for COMM 106M if taken after COMM 106MR.

nodes.title: Journalism and the News Industry
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: Survey the development of journalism as a profession and news media as an industry and social institution. How to understand the production of news, the forces that shape social representations in the news, access to the public sphere, and approaches to the analysis of news media content. Debates about ethical issues in journalism, “objectivity” and the politics of news, and the sustainability of journalism as an institution. No credit for COMM 106N if taken after COMM 106NR.

nodes.title: TV Industry
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): Any TWO additional courses numbered in the COMM 106 series
nodes.description: This course examines the political economy of television throughout its history. How TV is made, who is involved, how is industry organized, how does it get regulated, distributed? Consider how these answers changed over time and look at recent influences of digital technologies. No credit for COMM 106V if taken after COMM 106VR.

nodes.title: CSI: Communication and Social Institutions: Human Rights Advocacy: Journalists, Activists and Scholars at Risk
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: How should we respond to the continued violation of human rights to exercise freedom of expression and to engage in open inquiry and social justice actions without fear of persecution? Students will gain a practical understanding of the mechanisms through which different actors fight for human rights by researching and/or participating in an international human rights advocacy campaign on behalf of a specific journalist, activist, or scholar at risk of expulsion, imprisonment, or death.

nodes.title: Journalistic Writing, Reporting, and Research
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: Introduction to the basics of journalistic writing, reporting, and research. Students will consider voice and bias and discuss the major issues facing journalists today. Opportunities to write and report in different modes and across a variety of media, may include podcasting, beat reporting, investigative journalism, multimedia features, and more.

nodes.title: AMP: News Media Workshop
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Designed for students working in student news organizations or off-campus internships or jobs in news, public relations, or public information. A workshop in news writing and news analysis.

nodes.title: Critical Design Practice/Advanced Studio
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10 or COGS 1 or DSGN 1 or ESYS 10 or POLI 10 or POLI 10D or USP 1.
nodes.description: This hands-on course introduces design as social and political transformation. In it, students will learn to analyze how designed objects and environments entail political assumptions and choices, working in groups to design an intervention into some aspect of collective life that concerns them. It will include a mixture of lectures and studio-based activities.

nodes.title: Critical Design Practice/Topic Studio
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Course builds on understanding design as political activity. Group work to design quarter-long projects that explore political role of design, include design in built environments, organizations, media technologies. Deepened capacities to design in public, for publics, with publics. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: Media Activism
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Practice course in residence within the communication department
Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: This course explores the way artists and media-makers intervene in the public sphere and influence debates about pressing social, economic, and political problems. Looking at a range of media formats, we study and compare the tactics, strategies, and effectiveness of different approaches. This survey of political art and media is intended to stoke students’ curiosity in the local and global problems addressed and inspire students to engage in their own form of media art and activism.

nodes.title: Political Economy and International Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: The character and forms of international communications. Emerging structures of international communications. The United States as the foremost international communicator. Differential impacts of the free flow of information and the unequal roles and needs of developed and developing economies in international communications.

nodes.title: Advanced Studies in Cultural Industries
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: We examine how people interact with products of popular culture, production of cultural goods by looking at conditions in cultural industries. We examine film, music, publishing, focusing on how production is organized, what kind of working conditions arise, how products are distributed.

nodes.title: Concepts of Freedom
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: This course examines some of the changing cultural, social, technological, and political meanings; practices; and aspirations that together constitute what is and has been called freedom.

nodes.title: Behind the Internet: Invisible Geographies of Power and Inequality
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: This course aims to unveil the vast and largely hidden infrastructures silently shaping how digital communication take place in contemporary societies as well as the visible and invisible geographic of power and inequality these infrastructures are helping to create.

nodes.title: Surveillance, Media, and the Risk Society
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Contributions of the field of communication to the study of surveillance and risk. Critical and legal perspectives on consumer research, copyright enforcement, the surveillance capacity of Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs), closed-circuit television, interactive media, and the “rhetorics of surveillance” in television and film.

nodes.title: Bilingual Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: This course is designed to introduce students to multiple settings where bilingualism is the mode of communication. Examination of how such settings are socially constructed and culturally based. Language policy, bilingual education, and linguistic minorities, as well as field activities included.

nodes.title: Biography and Life Stories
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Course examines several different ways of telling stories as a form of communication: our own life and about the lives of others. There are also the occasions that the life stories of ordinary people are told at and celebrated, for example, funerals, Festschrifts, retirement dinners, fiftieth-anniversary parties, and retrospective art shows.

nodes.title: Environmental Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Survey of the communication practices found in environment controversies. The sociological aspects of environmental issues will provide background for the investigation of environmental disputes in particular contested areas, such as scientific institutions, communities, workplaces, governments, popular culture, and the media.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Mediation and Interaction
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Specialized advanced study in mediation and interaction with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. May be taken three times for credit.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Advanced study of a current topic in the discipline of communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Topic and description provided by the department quarterly. May be taken for credit up to three times. Students may receive a combined total of twelve units for COMM 172T and COMM 172TR.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Advanced study of a current topic in the discipline of communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Topic and description provided by the department quarterly. This is a distance education course. May be taken for credit up to three times. Students may receive a combined total of twelve units for COMM 172TR and COMM 172T.

nodes.title: Interaction with Technology
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: In this class we will look closely at the everyday ways in which we interact with technology to discuss sociocultural character of objects, built environments; situated, distributed, and embodied character of knowledges; use of multimodal semiotic resources, talk, gesture, body orientation, and gaze in interaction with technology.

nodes.title: Communication and Social Machines
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: An examination of the questions that developments in robotics pose to the scholars of communication: How do we communicate when our interlocutors are nonhumans? How do we study objects that are claimed to be endowed with social and affective character?

nodes.title: Cultures of Consumption
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: This course examines the cultural politics of consumption across time and cultures through several concepts: commodity fetishism; conspicuous consumption; taste; class; and identity formation; consumption’s psychological, phenomenological, and poetic dimensions; and contemporary manifestations of globalization and consumer activism.

nodes.title: Communication and Religion
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: The secularization thesis—that as society becomes more modern and standards of living rise, the importance of religion will diminish and be confined to the private sphere—may be wrong. We address religion, communication, culture, and politics in the United States.

nodes.title: Culture, Domination, and Resistance
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Explores theories and narratives of cultural power, contemporary practices of resistance. Texts from a wide range of disciplines consider how domination is enacted, enforced, and what modes of resistance are employed to contend with uses and abuses of political power.

nodes.title: Communication and Nonhuman Animals
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: The course increases our awareness of communicative repertoires in nonhuman animals. Noticing their richness allows us to engage topics of iconicity and indexicality, body and movement, feeling and sensation, space and environment, and aspects of voice that do not stand for established units of meaning. We will discuss how this turning to nonhuman communication illuminates human communication and how cross-species communication takes place.

nodes.title: Advanced Studies in Communication Theory
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: How are messages created, transmitted, and received? What is the relationship between thinking and communicating? How are linguistic processes embedded in sociocultural practices? Course discusses classic texts in the field of communication theory stemming from linguistics, semiotics, philosophy of language, literary theory.

nodes.title: Citizen Consumers
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: This course considers the idea of the citizen-consumer that organizes much of contemporary urban planning and processes of identity, class, race, and gender formation in cities globally. Focusing on contemporary service oriented economies, we will critically explore how consumption spaces, such as shopping malls, theme parks, plazas, markets, parks, beaches, and tourist resorts, are critical nodes to understand neoliberal patterns of land transformation, labor exploitation, and social change.

nodes.title: Education and Global Citizenship
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Concepts, possibilities, and dilemmas inherent in the notion of global citizenship. Formulate goals and instructional strategies for global education, expected competence of individuals within society. Examine roles that communication and curriculum play in the formation of identity, language use, and civic responsibility of global citizens.

nodes.title: Global Economy and Consumer Culture
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: This course critically examines social and economic forces that shape the making of this new global consumer culture by following the flows of consumption and production between the developed and developing worlds in the 1990s. We will consider how consumers, workers, and citizens participate in a new globalized consumer culture that challenges older distinctions between the First and the Third World. In this course, we will focus on the flows between the United States, Asia, and Latin America.

nodes.title: Global Nature/Global Culture
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: Considers globalization’s impact on concepts of nature in and through media texts, information systems, circulation of consumer goods and services, the emergence of global brands, science, health initiatives, environmental media activism, technology transfer in the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

nodes.title: Communication for Indigenous Justice
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: The course provides students the opportunity to learn from indigenous scholarship, activism, and art. It introduces students to indigenous justice issues such as knowledge production, environmental stewardship, cultural appropriation, and stereotyped representations—all within the contexts of settler colonialism and indigenous resistance and survival. It gives students tools to examine those issues from communication and media studies perspectives and to explore ways to promote indigenous justice.

nodes.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). No credit for COMM 190 if taken after COMM 190R.

nodes.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
groups: Upper-Division Electives (nine courses): THREE courses numbered from COMM 160–190
nodes.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 190R if taken after COMM 190.

nodes.title: Fluency in Information Technology
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduces the concepts and skills necessary to effectively use information technology. Includes basic concepts and some practical skills with computer and networks.

nodes.title: Introduction to Computer Science and Object-Oriented Programming: Python
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: An introduction to computer science and programming using the Python language. The course will cover topics such as basic data types (e.g., integer, float, string), loops and iteration, basic data structures (e.g., list, set, dictionary), memory models, conditional statements, recursion, basic algorithm time complexity analysis, class design, and inheritance. A student may not receive credit for CSE 6R after receiving credit for CSE 8A, CSE 8B, CSE 11, or COGS 18. Students may receive credit for only one of the following: COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: a familiarity with high school-level algebra is expected, but this course assumes no prior programming knowledge or experience.

nodes.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving I
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introductory course for students interested in computer science and programming. Basics of programming including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods. Structured data storage such as arrays/lists and dictionaries, including data mutation. Hands-on experience with designing, writing, hand-tracing, compiling or interpreting, executing, testing, and debugging programs. Students solve relevant computational problems using a high-level programming language. CSE 8A is part of a two-course sequence (CSE 8A-B) that is equivalent to CSE 11. Students should take CSE 8B to complete the CSE 8A/CSE 8B track. Students who have taken CSE 8B or CSE 11 may not take or receive credit for CSE 8A. Students may receive credit for one of the following: COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: No prior programming experience is assumed, but comfort using computers is helpful. Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing which CSE course to take first.

nodes.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving: Accelerated Pace
nodes.description: Accelerated introductory programming including an object-oriented approach. Covers basic programming topics from CSE 8A including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods, structured data storage, and mutation. Also covers topics from CSE 8B including the Java programming language, class design, interfaces, basic class hierarchies, recursion, event-based programming, and file I/O. Basics of command-line navigation for file management and running programs. Zero units of credit offered for CSE 11 if CSE 8B taken previously or concurrently. Recommended preparation: Significant prior programming experience (for example, high school AP CSA). Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing a first CSE course.

nodes.title: Introductory Programming for Computational Social Science
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course develops computational thinking practices and skills critical for defining, describing, and analyzing social science problems using a computational approach. Students will learn to program in Python in the context of computational social science problems.

nodes.title: Dimensions of Culture: Diversity
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement or concurrent enrollment in AWP 3, Analytical Writing.

requires.text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement in AWP 3

nodes.description: This course focuses on sociocultural diversity in examining class, ethnicity, race, gender, and sexuality as significant markers of differences among persons. Emphasizing American society while cultivating students’ critical reading skills, it explores the cultural understandings of diversity and its economic, moral, and political consequences. Restrictions: Marshall College students only, must be taken for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Dimensions of Culture: Justice
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement and completion of DOC 1. Enrollment by department approval only.

items.text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement
department approval

nodes.description: This course considers the nature of justice in philosophical, historical, and legal terms. Topics include racial justice, political representation, economic justice, gender and justice, the rights of cultural minorities, and crime and punishment. The course offers intensive instruction in writing university-level expository prose, specifically thesis-based argumentative essays. Restrictions: Marshall College students only, must be taken for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Dimensions of Culture: Imagination
nodes.description: This course examines the relevance of sociocultural diversity and the nature of justice in explicitly local and contemporary contexts. Students are asked to imagine and propose rigorously researched and interdisciplinary solutions to issues relevant to their own lived experiences. The course offers intensive instruction in writing university-level expository prose, with special emphasis on developing a research process. Restrictions: Marshall College students only, must be taken for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Principles of Data Science
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This first course in data science introduces students to data exploration, statistical inference, and prediction. It introduces the Python programming language as a tool for tabular data manipulation, visualization, and simulation. Through homework assignments and projects, students are given an opportunity to develop their analytical skills while working with real-world datasets from a variety of domains.

nodes.title: Principles of Data Science
nodes.description: This first course in data science introduces students to data exploration, statistical inference, and prediction. It introduces the Python programming language as a tool for tabular data manipulation, visualization, and simulation. Through homework assignments and projects, students are given an opportunity to develop their analytical skills while working with real-world datasets from a variety of domains.

nodes.title: Programming and Basic Data Structures for Data Science
nodes.prereq_text: DSC 10/R. Restricted to students within the data science or business data science major.

items.text: Restricted to students within the data science or business data science major

nodes.description: Provides an understanding of the structures that underlie the programs, algorithms, and languages used in data science by expanding the repertoire of computational concepts introduced in DSC 10/R and exposing students to techniques of abstraction. Course will be taught in Python and will cover topics including recursion, higher-order functions, function composition, object-oriented programming, interpreters, classes, and simple data structures such as arrays, lists, and linked lists.

nodes.title: Design of Everyday Things
nodes.description: A project-based course examining how principles from cognitive science apply to the design of things simple (doors) and complex (new technology). Learn about affordances, constraints, mappings, and conceptual models. Learn observational and design skills. Become a human-centered design thinker.

nodes.title: Principles of Microeconomics
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduction to the study of the economic system. Course will introduce the standard economic models used to examine how individuals and firms make decisions in perfectly competitive markets, and how these decisions affect supply and demand in output markets.

nodes.title: Financial Accounting
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: (Cross-listed with MGT 4.) Recording, organizing, and communicating financial information relating to business entities. Credit not allowed for both ECON 4 and MGT 4.

nodes.title: Data Analytics for the Social Sciences
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: (Cross-listed with POLI 5D.) Students engage in hands-on learning with applied social science problems. The course teaches the basics of data management and collection, data analysis, and data visualization. To perform these analyses, students learn how to code in various programming software, including Excel, Stata, and R. Students may receive credit for only one of the following courses: ECON 5, POLI 5, POLI 5D, ECON 5R.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Systems
nodes.description: This course explores the interdisciplinary character of environmental issues through an examination of a particular topic (climate change, for example) from numerous disciplinary perspectives (e.g., biology, chemistry, physics, political science, and economics).

nodes.title: The Ancient Mediterranean World
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of the UC Entry Level Writing requirement; open to Revelle students only.

items.text: satisfaction of the UC Entry Level Writing requirement
open to Revelle students only

nodes.description: Through the study of selected core texts in literature, philosophy, drama, history, and art, this course introduces students to the humanities and the cultures of the ancient Mediterranean that were integral to the formation of the Western intellectual tradition and have helped shape our modern world. Revelle students must take the course for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Rome and the Medieval World
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of the UC Entry Level Writing requirement; open to Revelle students only.

items.text: satisfaction of the UC Entry Level Writing requirement
open to Revelle students only

nodes.description: Through the study of selected core texts, this course explores the history and culture of Rome and the transition from antiquity to the medieval world. It examines the emergence of new ideas and forms of cultural expression in philosophy, literature, religion, and art from several traditions, including the Greco-Roman, Judeo-Christian, Islamic, and Germanic. Revelle students must take the course for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Writing Fiction
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: CAT 2 and 3 or CCE 1 and 2 or DOC 2 and 3 or HUM 1 and 2 or MCWP 40 and 50 or MMW 12 and 13 or WARR 11A-B or WCWP 10A-B or SYN 1 and 2.
nodes.description: Study of fiction in both theory and practice. Narrative technique studied in terms of subjectivity and atmosphere, description, dialogue, and the editing process will be introduced through readings from the history of the novel and short story. Students are required to attend at least three New Writing Series readings during the quarter.

nodes.title: Writing Poetry
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: CAT 2 and 3 or CCE 1 and 2 or DOC 2 and 3 or HUM 1 and 2 or MCWP 40 and 50 or MMW 12 and 13 or WARR 11A-B or WCWP 10A-B or SYN 1 and 2.
nodes.description: Study and practice of poetry as artistic and communal expression. Techniques of composition (traditional forms, avant garde techniques, dramatic monologue, performance poetry, and new genre) studied through written and spoken examples of poetry. Students are required to attend at least three New Writing Series readings during the quarter.

nodes.title: Writing Nonfiction
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: CAT 2 and 3 or CCE 1 and 2 or DOC 2 and 3 or HUM 1 and 2 or MCWP 40 and 50 or MMW 12 and 13 or WARR 11A-B or WCWP 10A-B or SYN 1 and 2.
nodes.description: Study of nonfictional prose in terms of genre and craft. Techniques of composition (journalism, essay, letters, reviews) will be studied through written examples of the genre.

nodes.title: Screen Writing Craft
nodes.description: A reading and craft class designed to encourage writing of original screenplays and adaptations. There will be analysis and discussion of representative examples of screen writing. Readings and lectures will accompany writing exercises. Restricted to LIT-BA-009 and LIT-BA-017 majors and LIT-MN-005 and LIT-MN-015 minors during first pass of registration. All other students may register during second pass of registration with the approval of the department.

nodes.title: Screen Writing Workshop
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: A workshop designed to encourage writing of original screenplays and adaptations. Class will focus primarily on the discussion of student work. Renumbered from LTWR 110. LTWR 110W may only be taken once for credit. No credit given for LTWR 110W if prior credit was earned three times for LTWR 110. Restricted to LIT-BA-009 and LIT-BA-017 majors and LIT-MN-005 and LIT-MN-015 minors during first pass of registration. All other students may register during second pass of registration with the approval of the department.

nodes.title: Critical Writing
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of Entry Level Writing Requirement.

requires.text: satisfaction of Entry Level Writing Requirement

nodes.description: First course of sequence in university reading and writing which satisfies the Muir College graduation requirement in writing. Required of all Muir College first-year students and of transfer students who have not completed a comparable course elsewhere. MCWP 40 introduces students to the basic elements of argument and analysis. Students engage in close reading of texts, weekly writing and revision, and individual conferences. Grades of C or higher are required for prerequisites. Students must take MCWP 40 for a letter grade to count toward the Muir College writing requirement. Students may receive credit for one of the following: MCWP 40, MCWP 40R, MCWP 40C, or MCWP 40CR.

nodes.title: Critical Writing
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of the MCWP 40 requirement or completion of IGETC.

items.text: completion of IGETC

nodes.description: Second course of sequence in reading and writing which satisfies the Muir College graduation requirement in writing. Required of all Muir College first-year students and of transfer students. MCWP 50 focuses on advanced skills of argument and analysis. Students engage in close reading of texts, weekly writing and revision, and individual conferences. Students will not receive credit for both MCWP 50 and MCWP 50R. Must be taken for a letter grade to satisfy the Muir College writing requirement.

nodes.title: Quantitative Methods in Business
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduction to techniques to develop/analyze data for informed tactical and strategic management decisions: statistical inference, probability, regression analysis, and optimization. Using these analytic approaches, theory-based formulas, and spreadsheets, students explore managerial applications across all areas of business activity.

nodes.title: Principles of Accounting
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Covers the principles, methods and applications of general accounting, cost accounting and investment ROI. Development of the three key financial reports and their interrelations, cost identification, product costing, inventory control, operational performance, and investment return

nodes.title: Product Marketing and Management
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Defining markets for products and services, segmenting these markets, and targeting critical customers within segments. Strategies to position products and services within segments. The critical role of pricing as well as market research, product management, promotion, selling, and customer support.

nodes.title: Negotiations
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course takes a decision-making orientation to negotiation. The course will build cumulatively from (seemingly) simple negotiations to those of greater complexity. These structured negotiation exercises are used to isolate and emphasize specific analytic points and essential skills. Cases and readings should help the student to integrate the analysis as well as to develop intuition about more complex negotiations. Students will not receive credit for both MGT 162 and MGT 162R.

nodes.title: Business Project Management
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Addresses effective practices for management of business projects. Includes both project management processes—scheduling, milestone setting, resource allocation, budgeting, risk mitigation—and human capital management—communication, teamwork, leadership. Also considers requirements for effectively working across functional and organizational boundaries. Students will not receive credit for both MGT 172 and MGT 172R.

nodes.title: Transforming Traditions and Emerging World Communities, circa 100 BCE–1200 CE
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing Requirement.

requires.text: satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing Requirement

nodes.description: This course provides a global perspective on the past from circa 100 BCE to circa 1200 CE, examining the emergence of interregional networks and empires and their relationship with the advent and expansion of diverse religious movements, including Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, as well as cross-cultural contacts and exchanges. The course also explores forms of identity (ethnic, religious, and other); models of inclusion and exclusion; systems of power, hierarchy, and slavery; and the human-environmental relationship. MMW 12 is the first of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 12 and MMW 12R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

nodes.title: Transforming Traditions and Emerging World Communities, circa 100 BCE–1200 CE
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing Requirement.

requires.text: satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing Requirement

nodes.description: MMW 12R is a distance education course. This course provides a global perspective on the past from circa 100 BCE to circa 1200 CE, examining the emergence of interregional networks and empires and their relationship with the advent and expansion of diverse religious movements, including Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, as well as cross-cultural contacts and exchanges. The course also explores forms of identity (ethnic, religious, and other); models of inclusion and exclusion; systems of power, hierarchy, and slavery; and the human-environmental relationship. MMW 12 is the first of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 12 and MMW 12R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

nodes.title: A Globalizing World: Exchanges, Entanglements, and Exploitation, Thirteenth–Eighteenth Century
nodes.prereq_text: MMW 12 or MMW 12R with a grade of D or better.
nodes.description: This course presents a global perspective on the connections, exchanges, and transformations that linked Afro-Eurasia and the Americas during the period from 1200 to 1750 CE. The course examines the nature and consequences of this increasingly connected world. It focuses on spaces of cross-cultural contact and exchange, including the transfer of technologies, ideas, commodities, and customs and their environmental impact; encounters in the form of travel, trade, migration, and invasion; and exploitation through empire, colonization, and slavery, and their manifestation in state violence, intolerance, discrimination, and racism. MMW 13 is the second of two writing-intensive courses in the MMW sequence. Students may not receive credit for both MMW 13 and MMW 13R. Open to Eleanor Roosevelt College (ERC) students only. Must be taken for a letter grade to meet the ERC graduation requirement.

nodes.title: Fundamentals of Music A
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course, first in a three-quarter sequence, is primarily intended for students without previous musical experience. It introduces music notation and basic music theory topics such as intervals, scales, keys, and chords, as well as basic rhythm skills.

nodes.title: Data Analytics for the Social Sciences
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduction to probability and analysis for understanding data in the social world. Students engage in hands-on learning with applied social science problems. Basics of probability, visual display of data, data collection and management, hypothesis testing, and computation. Students may receive credit for only one of the following courses: ECON 5, ECON 5R, POLI 5, POLI 5R, POLI 5D, or POLI 5DR.

nodes.title: Introduction to Political Science: American Politics
nodes.description: This course surveys the processes and institutions of American politics. Among the topics discussed are individual political attitudes and values, political participation, voting, parties, interest groups, Congress, presidency, Supreme Court, the federal bureaucracy, and domestic and foreign policy making. POLI 10 is Lecture only, and POLI 10D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 10 and 10D.

nodes.title: Introduction to Political Science: American Politics
nodes.description: This course surveys the processes and institutions of American politics. Among the topics discussed are individual political attitudes and values, political participation, voting, parties, interest groups, Congress, presidency, Supreme Court, the federal bureaucracy, and domestic and foreign policy making. POLI 10 is Lecture only, and POLI 10D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 10 and 10D.

nodes.title: Political Inquiry
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduction to the logic of inference in social science and to quantitative analysis in political science and public policy including research design, data collection, data description and computer graphics, and the logic of statistical inference (including linear regression). POLI 30 is Lecture only, and POLI 30D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 30 and 30D.

nodes.title: Political Inquiry
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Introduction to the logic of inference in social science and to quantitative analysis in political science and public policy including research design, data collection, data description and computer graphics, and the logic of statistical inference (including linear regression). POLI 30 is Lecture only, and POLI 30D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 30 and 30D.

nodes.title: Introduction to Statistics
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course provides an introduction to both descriptive and inferential statistics, core tools in the process of scientific discovery and the interpretation of research.

nodes.title: The Practice of Social Research
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of the design of social research. It examines the key varieties of evidence, sampling methods, logic of comparison, and causal reasoning researchers use in their study of social issues. Will not receive credit for SOCI 60 and SOCL 60.

nodes.title: Qualitative Interviewing
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course provides students with tools to conduct original research using qualitative interviews. Students will learn how to prepare, conduct, and analyze qualitative interviews. Special emphasis will be placed on the presentation of research in written form.

nodes.title: Research Reporting
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Students learn to write a research report/article. Course covers the architecture of reports, different audiences, scientific writing style, the literature review, and how to present methodology and findings. Students write a research report using research they conducted in other classes.

nodes.title: Communicating for a Changing Planet
nodes.prereq_text: Seventh College students only, completion of UC Entry Level Writing requirement, must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Seventh College general-education requirements.

items.text: Seventh College students only
completion of UC Entry Level Writing requirement

nodes.description: Synthesis 1 asks students to critically examine through an interdisciplinary and antiracist lens how we communicate about the climate crisis in order to address the question of how we get people to respond and take action. Through a variety of assignments and activities, students develop an awareness of both the message of a text and how the author crafted that message. They learn how to assess the purpose, audience, and context of different rhetorical situations.

nodes.title: Communicating for a Changing Planet
nodes.prereq_text: Seventh College students only, completion of UC Entry Level Writing requirement, must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Seventh College general-education requirements.

items.text: Seventh College students only
completion of UC Entry Level Writing requirement

nodes.description: Synthesis 1R asks students to critically examine through an interdisciplinary and antiracist lens how we communicate about the climate crisis in order to address the question of how we get people to respond and take action. Through a variety of assignments and activities, students develop an awareness of both the message of a text and how the author crafted that message. They learn how to assess the purpose, audience, and context of different rhetorical situations.

nodes.title: Inquiring about a Changing Planet
nodes.prereq_text: Seventh College students only, SYN 1/1R, must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Seventh College general-education requirements.

items.text: Seventh College students only

nodes.description: Synthesis 2 builds upon the skills developed in Synthesis 1. In the first half of the quarter, students learn the links between climate change and racial justice. Using an antiracist framework, students work in a small group to research an aspect of the climate crisis. In the second half of the quarter, students are introduced to project design and learn how to draft a proposal. Students learn how to determine the scope of a project based on such criteria as time, money, and potential impact.

nodes.title: Introduction to Acting
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: A beginning course in the fundamentals of acting: establishing a working vocabulary and acquiring the basic skills of the acting process. Through exercises, compositions, and improvisations, the student actor explores the imagination as the actor’s primary resource, and the basic approach to text through action.

nodes.title: Introduction to Design for the Theatre
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: A survey of contemporary and historical concepts and practices in the visual arts of the theatre; studies in text analysis, studio processes and technical production; elementary work in design criticism, scale model making, and costume design. A course serving as an introduction to theatre design and production.

nodes.title: Introduction to Dance Making
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Explores the concepts and processes of dance making through creative projects, discussions, and the examination of major dance works. Recommended preparation: No prior dance experience required. Open to all levels.

nodes.title: Stage Management
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Discussion and research into the duties, responsibilities, and roles of a stage manager. Work to include studies in script analysis, communication, rehearsal procedures, performance skills, and style and conceptual approach to theatre. THGE or TDGE 1, THAC or TDAC 1, and THDE or TDDE 1 recommended.

nodes.title: Introduction to Theatre
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: An introduction to fundamental concepts in drama and performance. Students will attend performances and learn about how the theatre functions as an art and as an industry in today’s world.

nodes.title: Cultivating the Creative Mind
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course will use the theatrical context to integrate scientific research about creativity, group dynamics, and related topics. Through a mix of theoretical and experiential classes and assignments, we will explore the intersection of theatre and neuroscience, investigating and expanding the creative mind.

nodes.title: Introduction to Playwriting
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Beginning workshop in the fundamentals of playwriting. Students discuss material from a workbook that elucidates the basic principles of playwriting, do exercises designed to help them put those principles into creative practice, and are guided through the various stages of the playwriting process that culminate with in-class readings of the short plays they have completed.

nodes.title: History of US Urban Communities
nodes.description: This course charts the development of urban communities across the United States both temporally and geographically. It examines the patterns of cleavage, conflict, convergence of interest, and consensus that have structured urban life. Social, cultural, and economic forces will be analyzed for the roles they have played in shaping the diverse communities of America’s cities.

nodes.title: Introduction to Art Making: Two-Dimensional Practices
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: An introduction to the concepts and techniques of two-dimensional art making with an emphasis on drawing. Lectures will introduce skills and concepts of contemporary drawing practice in relation to a variety of genres such as illustration, comics, advertising, animation, and other forms of visualization. This course is offered only one time each year.

nodes.title: Introduction to Art Making: Motion and Time-Based Art
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: A survey of time-based practices in contemporary art, including moving image, performance, and project-based work. Focusing on the passage of time as a component of art making, this class explores ways artists use time as material, concept, and foundation for methodology. This class introduces theoretical and art historical models for understanding how time is perceived within visual art forms and offers instruction in student development of their own time-based artworks. This course is offered only one time each year.

nodes.title: Introduction to Art Making: Three-Dimensional Practices
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: An idea-driven introduction to contemporary art practice, covering three-dimensional work relating to transformation, representation, workmanship, design, movement, time, and context. Students are asked to think openly and critically about art, and to articulate their ideas in physical form using various materials and products. This course is offered only one time each year.

nodes.title: Introduction to Digital Photography for Non-Majors
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course is a general study of the camera and photography utilizing digital technology. Emphasis is placed on developing fundamental manual control, understanding composition, and basic photographic techniques through lectures and field exercises.

nodes.title: Computing in the Arts Lecture Series
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Designed around presentations by visiting artists, critics, and scientists involved with contemporary issues related to computer arts and design. Lectures by the instructor and contextual readings provide background material for the visitor presentations. Program or materials fees may apply. Students may not receive credit for both VIS 10 and ICAM 110. This course is offered only one time each year.

nodes.title: Design Communication
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: This course provides a strong foundation in contemporary techniques of design communication, introduced in light of their significance to visual culture and the speculative design field. We cover digital image editing, typography, vector-based illustration and diagramming, and document layout. Also introduced are basic digital video editing tools and web production formats. Emphasis is on mastery of craft through iteration and presentation of multiple projects.

nodes.title: Introduction to Creative Coding
nodes.description: This course provides students with a foundation in programming and computational thinking, and their application in creative projects. Topics covered may include generative graphics and sound, interactive media, and others. Students will gain practical skills through hands-on experience and experimentation, learning to integrate computing into artistic practices.

nodes.title: Introduction to Media
nodes.prereq_text: none. Open to visual arts and cinematic arts majors and minors.

requires.text: Open to visual arts and cinematic arts majors and minors

nodes.description: Operating as both a lecture and production course, this introductory class provides a technical foundation and theoretical context for all subsequent production-oriented film and video studies. In the laboratory, the student will learn the basic skills necessary to initiate video production. Completion of Visual Arts 70N is necessary to obtain a media card. Program or materials fees may apply.

nodes.title: Practices in Computing Arts
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.prereq_text: VIS 42 or BILD 62 or COGS 18 or CSE 6R or CSE 8A or CSE 11 or DSC 20, upper-division standing.

items.text: upper-division standing

nodes.description: A survey of the conceptual uses and historical precedents for the use of computers in art and design. Preparation for further study in the computing in the arts area by providing an introduction to ideation strategies and critique-based evaluation, and an overview of theoretical issues related to the use of computers by artists and designers. Introduces the students to the program’s computing and production facilities, and basic computer programming skills. Two production-course limitation. Program or materials fees may apply.

nodes.title: Visualizing Art Practice
groups: Practice Courses (two courses): Second practice course
nodes.description: Artistic practice is a site of critical intervention. Through individual “Practice Diagrams,” students will visualize the issues, motivations, positions, and procedures that inspire and problematize their work, seeking to discover and mobilize new tools, spaces of research, and media experimentation.

nodes.title: The Writing Course A
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of the UC Entry Level Writing Requirement and must be a Warren College student.

items.text: satisfaction of the UC Entry Level Writing Requirement
must be a Warren College student

nodes.description: A seminar-style course in reading and writing required of all Warren College students. The course emphasizes argumentation and critical writing based on sources. Letter grades only.

nodes.title: The Writing Course B
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of WCWP 10A and must be a Warren College student.

items.text: must be a Warren College student

nodes.description: A seminar-style course in reading and writing required of all Warren College students who have completed WCWP 10A. The course continues the emphasis on argumentation and critical writing based on sources. Letter grades only.
